summary: Discusses deployment issues and requirements for successful mobile email that are implicit in the IETF lemonade documents. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Reading email on a phone works best when the mail server is set up the right way. This memo is a checklist for the people who run those servers.

questions: how to deploy mobile email with imap extensions
which ports does mobile imap need
why do nat timeouts break imap
subtitle: What networks, firewalls and NATs must allow so that mobile email over IMAP and Message Submission works.

tldr.problem: Lemonade mobile email depends on basics such as open ports, long-lived TCP connections and well-behaved firewalls and NATs that are generally assumed and rarely documented, and which have been reported to be problematic.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC states the requirements: IMAP on port 143 and Message Submission on port 587 must be reachable, TCP connections must not be cut for duration, and idle timeouts should be at least two hours.
tldr.outcome: It also warns against tunnelling new services over HTTP to dodge firewall policy and recommends TLS, DMZs and a threat analysis before exposing mail servers.

today: RFC 5383 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 143) and, according to the metadata for this site, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What This Document Covers
sections.content:
The IETF lemonade group developed a set of extensions to IMAP and Message Submission, plus a profile document that restricts server behavior and describes client usage (RFC 4550).

RFC 5383 explains that successful deployment of lemonade-compliant mobile email needs functionality that is generally assumed and therefore rarely covered in email RFCs. It describes these extra considerations, focusing on those reported to be problematic. It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 143).
sections.plainLanguage: Some things everybody assumes about the network are written down here, because they sometimes go wrong for phone email.

sections.title: Ports That Must Be Open
sections.content:
Both IMAP and Message Submission have well-known ports that MUST be available: IMAP uses port 143 and Message Submission uses port 587. The client and server systems, and any intermediaries, must allow communication on them.

Message User Agents historically used port 25 for submission, and RFC 4409 accommodates that. But ISPs and organizations increasingly restrict outbound port 25, and hotels sometimes intercept port 25 connections whatever the destination, so users may unknowingly submit sensitive mail to untrusted third-party servers. Application-level firewalls on SMTP also make new extensions harder to deploy on port 25. Lemonade clients should therefore use, and servers listen on, port 587 by default.

Lemonade also needs the Message Submission server to open a TCP connection to the IMAP server, for forward-without-download, by default on port 143. Clients may also need to reach configuration servers; the RFC gives ACAP (RFC 2244) on port 674 as an example.
sections.plainLanguage: Email uses special numbered doors. Those doors must be unlocked, and the old busy door 25 is not a safe choice.

sections.title: Long-Lived TCP Connections
sections.content:
Application use of TCP is REQUIRED of both client and server systems, and the Message Submission server must be able to connect to the IMAP server. Where only HTTP is available, webmail can be offered, but the RFC says that environment is by definition limited and cannot be lemonade compliant.

Connections between client and server can last arbitrarily long. The client, the server and all intermediate systems MUST NOT end these connections simply because of how long they have been open. Idle timers should be enforced only at the application level (IMAP and Message Submission). Because IMAP allows unsolicited notifications, clients can sensibly stay connected for long periods with no data flowing.

Two hours is a common middlebox idle timeout, so lemonade clients and servers SHOULD make sure a connection does not stay idle for two hours unless configured for a longer interval. The RFC also reports that some networks limit the duration of non-HTTP TCP connections and calls that harmful.

TCP should survive temporary loss of lower-level connectivity, such as handoffs or fade, when the client's IP address does not change. Lemonade systems SHOULD NOT set the TCP keep-alive option unless it works correctly and sends no more often than every two hours; application-level keep-alives such as IMAP NOOP may be used instead. Systems must also follow the rule that ICMP Destination Unreachable codes 0, 1 and 5 are soft errors that must not abort a TCP connection.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone line to the mail server should stay open for a long time without anyone hanging up just because it has been a while. If you must check in, do it rarely.

sections.title: Dormancy and Battery Life
sections.content:
Cellular data channels are connection-oriented, and setting them up costs network resources. In general a mobile device's battery lasts longer when the traffic channel is used less.

Some devices and networks support dormant mode, where the traffic channel is brought down during idle periods while the PPP or equivalent level stays active and the mobile keeps its IP address. Client, server and intermediate systems SHOULD keep TCP connections alive through dormancy, as described in the lifetime and transient-loss rules.

Sending packets only to keep a session alive repeatedly brings the channel up and lets it time out again. The RFC says that, without configuration to the contrary, this is still necessary by default to ensure correct operation.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone saves battery by napping between messages. Pointless pokes wake it up again and again, so the network should let the connection sleep instead.

sections.title: Firewalls and the Temptation to Tunnel
sections.content:
Proper deployment requires TCP connections from the client to the IMAP and Message Submission ports, and from the Message Submission server to the IMAP server, which may mean configuring firewalls. Firewalls MUST NOT damage protocol traffic, and MUST NOT partially block extensions, for example by allowing only one side of an extension negotiation, since the two sides then fall out of sync (see RFC 2979). The RFC also says one key way a new service helps secure deployment is keeping the one-to-one association of services and port numbers.

Teams often find the firewall group unwilling to open ports and are tempted to tunnel the new service over HTTP on port 80 or SMTP on port 25. This may look successful at first, but once the network security group notices, it will usually block it, causing collateral damage to the new service and to the existing service it was layered on (see RFC 3205). If a vulnerability is later found, both must be disabled until it is fixed. The RFC concludes that the delay of a proper review is likely cheaper in the long run than the kludge.
sections.plainLanguage: If the guard will not open the gate, sneaking through the kitchen door gets everybody in trouble. It is better to ask properly.

sections.title: NAT Timeouts
sections.content:
Any NAT boxes between client and server MUST comply with REQ-5 of RFC 5382, which requires the established connection idle-timeout to be not less than 2 hours 4 minutes.

IMAP and Message Submission clients reopen connections automatically, but this costs time, packets and processing: authentication, TLS negotiation, server work and a reset of TCP behavior such as windows. Forcing clients to send NOOP commands just to maintain NAT state is also wasteful and can defeat dormancy mode.
sections.plainLanguage: A NAT box must not forget a conversation too quickly. Two hours and four minutes is the shortest it is allowed to wait.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any organization exposing services to the Internet faces security considerations, and mobile email is no exception. The RFC advises doing a threat analysis, putting protections in place and then consciously deciding to open the service. Piggybacking on the HTTP port skips that step and reduces overall security.

As illustrations, the RFC mentions placing servers in DMZs, keeping authentication credentials on a system not reachable from the Internet, and using a DMZ IMAP server with no mail store of its own. It cautions that adding a gateway in front of mail servers may leave security unchanged or make it significantly worse.

Organizations SHOULD deploy servers that support TLS for all connections and can be configured to require it, preferably via STARTTLS rather than the alternate port method. TLS helps against eavesdropping and alteration, but its presence does not make a system secure.
sections.plainLanguage: Think about the dangers first, then open the door, and add a lock like TLS. A lock alone does not make a house safe.

items.label: IMAP
items.desc: Client to server, and Message Submission server to IMAP server.

items.label: Message Submission
items.desc: Default for lemonade clients and servers.

items.label: SMTP (legacy submission)
items.desc: Often restricted or intercepted; not the lemonade default.

items.title: No duration limits
items.text: Systems must not end connections just for being open a long time.

items.title: Two-hour idle rule
items.text: Do not let a connection sit idle for two hours by default.

items.title: Avoid TCP keep-alive
items.text: Prefer application-level keep-alives such as IMAP NOOP.
